fr:mainmatter.html:p: problem s ovom pricom je sto (valjda?) obicno korsitimo fundamnetalni poligon da dobijemo info o manifoldu, jer je poligon jednostavniji objekat. ili ipak ide u oba pravca?
The set of complex numbers C is not compact on its own, but we can compactify it (make it compact), just like we can do so with the real line R, which is also not compact on its own.

One way to compactify R is to add to it a point at infinity and obtain the set \overline \R = \R \cup \{\infty \} -- this is called the one-point compactification (distinguishing between \pm \infty yields a so called two-point compactification). Turns out, \overline \R is homeomorphic to a circle in the Euclidean plane, thus, the unit circle is a nice tangible model of \overline \R . If we put a circle on top of the real line, and let it touch the line at 0, and if we stereographically project (in 2D sense) all the points of the circle onto the line, we can get a 1-1 correspondence between all the points of the circle and the real line, except for one: the antipodal point of 0, which we call the north pole; for this \R won't do, but \overline \R will.

We can compactify \mathbb {C} in a similar manner: just do \overline \mathbb {C} = \mathbb {C} \cup \{\infty \}. A tangible model for this compactification is a sphere, also usually called the Riemann sphere. Conventions may vary, but we can think of it as a sphere placed on the complex plane, touching the xy-plane at 0,0,0, centered at {0,0,1}, with a diameter of 1. Then the north pole N is at the point 0,0,2. The reason why the Riemann sphere is indeed a model of \overline \mathbb {C} is again the stereographic projection; again, in order to map the north pole N somewhere, \mathbb {C} alone won't do, but in \overline \mathbb {C}, N has a natural place to map to: \infty .
A set D \subseteq \mathbb {C} that is both open and connected is called a domain.
Most results in complex analysis assume that the underlying set is a domain, so this is a key notion.
We say that a domain U is simply connected if the set \mathbb {C}\setminus U has no bounded components.
In other words, the domain has no holes. A useful characterisation is the theorem that says that U is simply connected iff \overline C \setminus U is connected.

A continuous curve in the complex plane is the image of a continuous complex mapping \gamma : [\alpha , \beta ] \to \mathbb {C}. It can be described with the equation: \gamma (t) = x(t) + iy(t), \quad t \in [\alpha , \beta ] where x, y are continuous real functions of t \in [\alpha , \beta ].
A curve has an orientation: for a positively oriented curve \gamma , we denote the same curve with clockwise orinetation with -\gamma .
A Jordan (or simple) curve \gamma is one that has no self intersections.

A continuous curve \gamma in the complex plane is smooth if it can be parametrised with t \in [\alpha , \beta ] with a continuously-differentiable mapping, whose derivative has no zeroes for t \in [\alpha , \beta ].
A piecewise smooth curve is a curve that is made of finitely many smooth curves. More idiomatically, we call such a curve a contour.

fr:title.text: Random notes on Tammo Tom Dieck's Algebraic Topology

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Random notes on Tammo Tom Dieck's Algebraic Topology

html:ul.html:li: Kolmogorov Quotients are always T_0 (or Kolmogorov spaces). Kolmogorov spaces are a reflective subcategory of topological spaces, the Kolmogorov quotient is the reflector.
Metrizable spaces have countable neighbourhood bases of points: Take the U_{\varepsilon } (x) with rational \varepsilon .

It has become clear to me now that \mathbb {R} is some kind of ruler and a reference structure for much of these developments. Perhaps just as \mathbb {N} was for \mathbb {R}, through \mathbb {Z} and further \mathbb {Q}. I'm stating a simple fact here, e.g., the codomain of a metric is \mathbb {R} (that's how we defined it), that's all. I never deeply internalised that the codomain for a metric can't be anything else. Which leads to the natural question, is there a generalisation of a metric wrt. its codomain, which can have something else for its codomain, or, must have an abstract object X, which must satisfy some properties, and so on.

This subsection could be efficiently summarised (mod embeddings talk) with this problem: Prove \mathbb {R} / \mathbb {Z} is homeomorphic to S^1. To solve it you need quotient mapping characterisation, you get to use the Universal Property of quotient maps, you get a hint of the algebra-topology interplay. (Also, you remind yourself of the open mapping theorem from complex analysis.)

fr:title.text: Intro to Galois theory, part 1: Algebraic (Field) Extensions

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Intro to Galois theory, part 1: Algebraic (Field) Extensions

fr:mainmatter.html:p: let me try and summarize the section Algebraic Extensions from Malik's fundamentals of abstract algebra. ill first outline the big picture: what role this section has in galois theory, then ill focus on the small picture: how do we build (algebraic) extensions of fields.
so we are still at the low stages of the theory building that will culminate in galois theory.

i find it hard to even start talking about the point of this section without spoiling the point of galois theory, thus mild spoiler alert:
galois theory gives us something useful about certain posets that we care about. (actually it's not posets but lattices, but close enough). what i will do here is talk about these "posets", the "something useful" part i wont be going into here.

we'll be working with fields. instead of saying that "K is a subfield of F", we'll be saying that "F/K is field extension of K". writing just F/K saves us a lot of time, but there are other benefits. we also read F/K as "F over K". example of usage: "let F/K be a field extension" = "let K be a field and F a field s.t. K is a subfield of F". the reason this notation makes this reversal is because we will indeed often be starting with K and constructing the field F from K; so we ascend from K to F.(spoiler: F will usually be a certain field that we denote with K(c), which does a better job at hinting that the extension K(c)/K is something that we actually built on top of K)

id say the main result of this section was the following: it turns out this "over" relation between F and K is a partial order, even though at this point we don't explicitly frame it that way. same with different words: the "extension" relation induces a poset on fields L: K\subseteq L\subseteq F. this is the poset that galois theory works its magic on. (i think this is roughly correct, im writing this for myself mostly so sorry not sorry for misleading stuff.)

so what's the deal with this poset? well we care about a specific kind of extension, namely a so called algebraic extension. ok we know F/K means F is an extension of K. we say that F/K is an *algebraic* extension of K if every element in F is algebraic over K. say a \in F is algebraic over K, that means the following: there's a (non-zero!) polynomial p(x) \in K[x] s.t. p(a) = 0. that's it. a is algebraic iff it's a zero of a polynomial with coefficients in K. so i might've lied earlier (unsure!), it's actually the relation "algebraic extension" that induces our poset, not merely the "over"/"extension" relation.
one of the very last theorems we prove in this section is basically transitivity for this relation: Theorem: F/K is algebraic iff F/L and L/K are algebraic.

what we said so far was contextualization for the big picture. so let me recenter this summary at this point and focus on the small picture of this section. say you stumble upon the innocent looking polynomial 2-x^2=p(x) \in \mathbb {Q}[x]. you notice that p(\sqrt 2) = 0, but \sqrt 2 \notin \mathbb {Q}. weird huh. may i suggest extending the field \mathbb {Q} via \sqrt 2, that we just saw is an algebraic element? but how do we do that?

so this section is about how we construct extensions of fields and algebraic extensions in particular. even more particular: it's about *extending* a given field K via an algebraic element c, so we want a field that contains K \uplus \{c\}.(remember that c is not in K, \sqrt 2 was not in \mathbb {Q}; all elements of K are algebraic over K (why? what polynomials in K are they solutions?)). this is now the usual situation where \cup doesn't preserve the algebraic structure, ie K \uplus \{c\} isn't a field (trust). but using the familiar trick/notation \langle \cdot \rangle for "generated by", \langle K \uplus \{c\}\rangle is a field that contains K \uplus \{c\}. so let's unpack what \langle K \uplus \{c\}\rangle actually is. it's the following thing: \langle K \uplus \{c\}\rangle = \{f(c) : f(x) \in K[x]\}. and as one might remember, \langle A\rangle is the same as the intersection of all fields (or any algebraic structure) that contain the field A, formally: \langle A\rangle = \bigcap _{B\supseteq A} B. connecting this with what we just said we have \bigcap _{F\supseteq K \uplus \{c\}} F = \langle K \uplus \{c\}\rangle = \{f(c) : f(x) \in K[x]\}.the meaning of this is that \langle K \uplus \{c\}\rangle = \{f(c) : f(x) \in K[x]\} is the *smallest* algebraic extension of K via c. and we are glad that it's smallest because any surplus would be expensive, we want to pay only for what we have to pay for; we want to be efficient (see: adjoints wiki, adjoint.tree (coming soon)). this also sheds a very bright ray of light on the purpose of polynomial rings, which i shall say more about later.

are there approaches to group theory that are a bit more global in the following sense: in the category set objects are sets. there are no constraints on what a subset (ill call it the substructure) of a set can be, as long as it satisfies the basic definition (contains only some (or all) elements of the parent set). in the category grp, the objects are groups, and we know that the order of the subgroup (subgroups are now the relevant substructure) has to divide the order of the group; however we know this is not sufficient, since no real analogue of lagrange theorem exists. so im wondering if group theory can be built by putting a constraint on what its substructure (subgroup) can be ? are there approaches to group theory like this that are similar in spirit?

what kind of category would we get if we just said: cardinality (order) of substructure has to divide the cardinality (order) of parent structure? i assume the category of finite groups would be a "subcategory" of this? has anyone done this? (see: fusion categories)
i really dont know much about it, but this is reminiscent to me of point free topology. is there point free group theory ?
(ofc the natural question onward would be: is there point free [insert structure here] theory?)
note: this came to mind after a brief convo w Asija, i was trying to explain why being able to see a group G as a subgroup of group of permutations is useful (subgroups divide order etc.)
